metadata.title: It's an Agent, Not a Command.
metadata.subtitle: Agent Development · Claude Code
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when you want a Claude Code plugin to handle a task on its own, is that a command or something else? Lands the carry-out that an agent is one file — a description with examples that decides when it runs, and a body that decides what it does.

beats.narration_text: Extending a plugin, you reach for 'command.' A command only fires when you type it. What you want here keeps running on its own, through several steps. That's an agent — one file builds it.

beats.narration_text: Here's what an agent actually is: one markdown file, split by a line of dashes. Above the line, YAML frontmatter — the agent's routing data. A name in lowercase-with-hyphens. A description, which Claude reads to decide when to fire this agent. A model field, almost always set to "inherit," meaning use whatever the parent session is using. A color, from a small fixed set tied to the kind of work. And an optional tools list — this is the trade-off worth naming: leave tools out and the agent inherits every tool there is; write a restricted list and you narrow its blast radius on purpose. Below the line, plain markdown, addressed straight at the agent — "you are," "you do" — and that text becomes the agent's system prompt.

production_viz.label: ONE FILE, TWO PARTS
production_viz.caption: the body below becomes the system prompt

beats.narration_text: The description field is what actually decides when this agent runs. Say you want one that reviews Python code for security issues. The pattern isn't free-form: "Use this agent when," followed by two to four worked examples, and each example has four parts — the setup, the user's message, what the agent would say back, and a note on why it fits. Here's the design choice worth naming: Claude isn't reading your intent, it's matching against those examples. Skip them and there's nothing for the trigger to bind to. The agent still exists in the folder; it just never fires.

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — THE TRIGGER
production_viz.caption: example: reviews Python code for security issues

beats.narration_text: The format is precise where it can be, open where it can't. Precise: names are lowercase with hyphens, examples take a fixed shape, and the body follows five sections — responsibilities, process, standards, output, edge cases. Open: the format doesn't decide which model tier to spend on, doesn't decide whether the task you're describing is really agent-shaped or just a command in disguise, and doesn't decide how one agent hands off to another. Those calls happen in the body text you write, not in the frontmatter. They optimized for lock-down at the frontier and judgment in the interior.

production_viz.label: PRECISE HERE, OPEN THERE
production_viz.caption: spelled out on the left; your call on the right

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Open a Claude Code session and paste this: Create an agent for my plugin that reviews Python code for security vulnerabilities. Then run the design-check — four things. Does the description start with "Use this agent when" and carry at least two examples? Is the model set to "inherit" rather than hardcoded to one? Is the tools list restricted to what a reviewer actually touches — reading and searching code, roughly — instead of omitted entirely? And does the body address the agent directly, in second person? Those four are your gate. Fail one and the agent won't behave like an agent; it'll behave like a broken command.

beats.narration_text: Here is a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. It gives any frontier LLM enough context to draft a real Claude Code agent file — full YAML frontmatter, trigger examples in the correct four-part shape, and a five-section body addressed to the agent in second person — for one specific job: a Python security reviewer. Go deeper: how would you split that single reviewer into two agents — one that finds issues, one that fixes them — and what specific handoff would you write into each body so they don't fight each other?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to write a Claude Code agent for my plugin. A Claude Code agent is a single markdown file with YAML frontmatter (name in lowercase-with-hyphens, a description that tells Claude when to fire the agent, a model field usually set to "inherit," a color from a small fixed set, and an optional tools list — leave it out and the agent inherits every tool) and a markdown body addressed to the agent in second person ("you are…," "you do…") that becomes its system prompt. The description follows a fixed pattern: "Use this agent when," then two to four worked examples, each with four parts — the setup, the user's message, what the agent would say back, and a note on why it fits. Draft a complete agent file for one job: reviewing Python code for common security issues (SQL injection, unsafe deserialization, hard-coded secrets, unvalidated input, insecure random for tokens). Give me the full YAML frontmatter, two to four trigger examples in the correct four-part shape, and a body with five sections — responsibilities, process, standards, output, edge cases — addressed to the agent in second person. Keep the tools list restricted to what a reviewer actually needs.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: how would you split that single security-reviewer into two agents — one that finds issues, one that fixes them — and what specific handoff would you write into each body so they don't fight each other or double-review the same code?
